openLegalQuestions.question: The complete current text of both provisions was obtained on this pass and CONFIRMS the single-node treatment. Miss. Code Ann. § 9-11-15(3), last amended by Laws 2016 ch. 406 § 1, and § 21-23-7(6), last amended by Laws 2021 ch. 356, are word-for-word identical on every operative element: prior notice to the prosecutor, a showing in open court of rehabilitation, good conduct for a period of two years since the last conviction IN ANY COURT and that the best interest of society would be served, discretionary relief, 'the record of conviction of a person of any or all misdemeanors in that court', the restoration-of-status and lawful-denial language, the carve-out for the confidential records of law-enforcement agencies, and the identical Title 63 driving-record limitation. They differ only in the court petitioned and in whether the county prosecutor or the municipal prosecuting attorney is noticed. Neither section specifies a fee. What remains open is local practice, not the statutory text.

Open question blocks release (filing_process): Local practice in the twenty-one circuit court districts other than the Fourth, and in every municipal and justice court, was not surveyed. Both the review and the Fourth District materials establish that districts maintain their own petition and order preferences and that some expect the district attorney to sign the order as approved as to form before the judge will sign. This is a scaling constraint rather than a legal one: the statutory mechanism is the same statewide, but the accepted document and the practical gate vary. Every Mississippi track therefore carries localFormOverride and a mandatory clerk-contact instruction.

Open question blocks release (filing_process): Whether the Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-72 fee reaches a given petition. The section reads: 'A filing fee of One Hundred Fifty Dollars ($150.00) is hereby levied on each petition to expunge an offense under Section 99-19-71 to be collected by the circuit clerk', distributed $100 to the Judicial System Operation Fund, $40 to the District Attorneys Operation Fund and $10 retained by the circuit clerk. Last amended by Laws, 1st Ex. Sess. 2017, ch. 7, § 12; no enacted amendment through 2026. Two things remain unresolved on its face and are NOT resolved by construction here. First, the trigger is 'each petition to expunge AN OFFENSE under Section 99-19-71': a § 99-19-71(4) non-conviction petition is a petition under § 99-19-71 but is not a petition to expunge an offence, because there is no conviction, and the statute does not settle it either way. Second, the collection mechanism names the CIRCUIT CLERK, which does not map onto § 99-19-71(1) or (4) petitions filed in justice or municipal court. Sections 9-11-15(3), 21-23-7(6), 99-15-26, 63-11-30, 41-29-150 and 67-3-70 sit outside § 99-19-71 and the fee does not reach them by its terms; none of those sections specifies a fee of its own. The packet therefore publishes NO fee amount on any track and instructs the participant to confirm the filing fee, and any pauper's-affidavit route, with the clerk of the court before filing.

Open question blocks release (governing_mechanism): Trafficking-survivor relief under Miss. Code Ann. § 97-3-54.6, as amended by 2026 HB 1546 effective 1 July 2026, is recorded here as a separately-listed matter and NOT as a tenth normalized source node, because neither the adopted Batch 2 memorandum nor the authoritative source crosswalk lists it among Mississippi's nine core adult slots. The enrolled text was read: new § 97-3-54.6(6) lets the sentencing court, at any time after a conviction or adjudication of delinquency of a misdemeanour or a felony not classified as a crime of violence under § 97-3-2, expunge on appropriate motion where it finds by a preponderance that participation in the offence occurred during the period the person was being trafficked and was the direct result of that trafficking; official documentation from a federal, state or local government agency creates a presumption but is not required; and new § 97-3-54.6(7)(b) provides that neither failing to raise the trafficking affirmative defence nor the court's finding on it affects the ability to file under subsection (6). This relief is broader and faster than ordinary § 99-19-71 conviction expungement, so screening for it belongs on every intake. Whether it becomes a normalized node requires an express crosswalk or memorandum instruction.

Open question blocks release (eligibility_branch): The complete current text of Miss. Code Ann. § 99-15-26 was obtained on this pass and resolves most of what the review left open. The section is the integration of two 2019 acts under § 1-1-109 — Laws 2019 ch. 362 § 4 and Laws 2019 ch. 466 § 41, the Criminal Justice Reform Act — with no enacted amendment since. Subsection (1)(a) covers felony and misdemeanour cases in circuit or county court on a guilty plea entered on or after 1 July 2014, OTHER THAN crimes against the person, a crime of violence as defined in § 97-3-2, a violation of § 97-11-31, or crimes in which a person unlawfully takes, obtains or misappropriates funds received by or entrusted to the person by virtue of public office or employment; (1)(b) covers misdemeanours in justice or municipal court; (1)(c) covers misdemeanour domestic violence in any of the four courts. Subsection (1)(d) makes the benefit ONCE-ONLY — 'No person having previously qualified under the provisions of this section shall be eligible to qualify for release in accordance with this section for a repeat offense' — and excludes trafficking under § 41-29-139(f) and any offence under the Implied Consent Law, which can only be nonadjudicated under § 63-11-30. Subsection (2) sets the conditions the court may impose, with good behaviour up to five years in circuit or county court and two years in justice or municipal court. Subsection (4) makes the DISMISSAL automatic: on successful completion the court 'shall direct that the cause be dismissed and the case be closed'. The expungement subsection is (5) as the review recorded, and it requires a petition. One textual gap survives and is preserved rather than resolved: § 99-15-26(5) and § 99-19-71(4) are near-verbatim twins, and BOTH are keyed to 'a case in which an arrest was made, the person arrested was released and the case was dismissed', which describes a pre-adjudication arrest-and-release posture rather than a post-guilty-plea nonadjudication dismissal under (4). Neither section says in terms that a subsection (4) dismissal is expungeable on petition.

Open question blocks release (governing_mechanism): Whether a successful nonadjudication dismissal requires its own petition under § 99-15-26, qualifies independently under § 99-19-71(4) as a case that was dismissed, or permits either route. This is the routing question and it is unresolved. The packet fails closed by pleading § 99-15-26 alone on this track, never merging the two statutes, and never reproducing the archived Fourth District dual citation.

Open question blocks release (correct_form): The complete current text was obtained on this pass and resolves the review's open questions on this track. The expungement provision is Miss. Code Ann. § 63-11-30(13), from enrolled SB 2095 (Laws 2022 ch. 303), which is the last enacted amendment — no 2023 to 2026 amendment touched it, and 2026 HB 1546 changed only § 99-19-71(2). Open question blocks release (governing_mechanism): The complete current text was obtained on this pass and closes the review's open question. The conditional discharge sits at Miss. Code Ann. § 41-29-150(d)(1) and the expungement remedy at § 41-29-150(d)(2); the last enacted amendment is Laws 2010 ch. 460 § 2 and there has been none since. Eligible offences are violations of § 41-29-139(c), simple possession, and § 41-29-139(d), paraphernalia; sale, distribution and manufacture under § 41-29-139(a) are outside the route, and the relief is unavailable where the court accepted the plea and adjudicated guilt. The prior-record restriction, the once-only limitation, the Bureau of Narcotics nonpublic record, the application procedure and the mandatory hearing are as summarised in the controlling authority. The section specifies no fee and § 99-19-72's fee does not reach it.

scopeRestrictions: This is the only one of the four additions that does NOT run through § 40-32-108, and it is the only Tennessee route in the entire chapter on which the participant writes the operative petition. Open question blocks release (eligibility_branch): The prior-expunction bars across the T.C.A. § 40-32-107 subsections are asymmetric on the enacted text and the asymmetry cannot be resolved from it. Subsections (a), (b) and (c) each bar a petitioner previously granted expunction under (a), (b) or (c), and name neither (d) nor (e). Subsection (e)(1)(D) bars a petitioner previously granted expunction under (a), (b), (c) or (e). Subsection (d) states no prior-expunction bar at all and is named by none of the others. AFFECTED TRACKS: tn_eligible_conviction, tn_two_offense, tn_post_pardon, tn_recovery_court and tn_illegal_voting. SCREENING IMPACT: the intake asks whether the participant has previously been granted expunction under (a), (b), (c) or (e) and records the answer, but no screen infers a bar that the subsection under which the participant is applying does not state, and in particular no bar is inferred against or from subsection (d). CURRENT PACKET TREATMENT: the packet reports the participant's own answer and states which bars the governing subsection actually contains; it asserts no conclusion about a subsection that is silent, and it does not tell a participant that a route is closed on the strength of a bar the statute does not impose. REQUIRED FUTURE CLARIFICATION: a statutory amendment naming the subsections reciprocally, or a counsel determination on whether a prior (e) grant closes (a), (b) and (c) and on whether any prior grant closes (d). RUNTIME EFFECT: none. tracks.publicName: Clear an eligible offence after finishing recovery court, where an old DUI is in the way
scopeRestrictions: LegalEase does not obtain the district attorney general's agreement, does not negotiate with that office, does not prepare or sign its petition or proposed order, does not create the TBI certificate or the TBI expungement order, does not create a clerk certification, makes no judicial finding, certifies no eligibility and promises neither filing nor relief. Refusal, opposition or disputed eligibility routes to an attorney handoff, and the participant still receives the generated request, the controlled factual record and the instructions before that handoff.

This is a relief-from-the-DUI-bar route, not a DUI-expunction route, and reading it the other way would be the single most damaging error available on it. A DUI under § 55-10-401 is itself expunction-ineligible and appears in the § 40-32-107(a)(1)(D) misdemeanour exclusion list, and § 40-32-107(e)(3) provides that a court shall not grant an expunction under the subsection if the offence sought to be expunged involves a motor vehicle and the use of alcohol or a controlled substance, including but not limited to a violation of § 55-10-401. What subsection (e) does is let a person who carries one DUI conviction expunge a different, otherwise-eligible offence committed at least ten years after it — relief that § 40-32-107(a)(3)(A) would otherwise deny, because that provision requires the offence to have occurred prior to any conviction for an expunction-ineligible offence.

legalDesignBlockers: Open question blocks the build (correct_form): Whether the Administrative Office of the Courts' Certificate of Restoration of Opportunity forms are mandatory forms a superior court must accept and a filer must use, pattern forms a filer may adapt, or optional. This reopens the question in the opposite direction from the memo's first pass, which concluded that no Washington Courts pattern form exists for an RCW 9.97.020 application: a complete statewide set has existed since 2016 under the RCW 9.97.020(11) duty — CRO 01.0100 petition, CRO 01.0200 notice, CRO 01.0300 proof of service, CRO 01.0700 order and certificate, with CRO 01.0600 the court's own dismissal order, plus instructions and a brochure. It is build-level because it decides whether this route is official_pdf_fill on the state's own forms or custom_pleading conforming to them. It is not answered here: the statutory word "sample" in RCW 9.97.020(11)(b) points toward pattern rather than mandatory, but the Washington court rule governing the status of Administrative Office of the Courts forms was not read, and this memo does not guess. The statute exempts criminal investigation reports and all records relating to offenses subject to section 15-12-1 et seq. because the person was found not guilty by reason of mental illness, intellectual disability, or addiction. That is a narrow not-guilty-by-reason-of carve-out, not a general sex-offense exclusion. Read the reference's way, it would wrongly bar people whose sex-offense charges were dismissed outright.

openLegalQuestions.question: Whether the § 61-11-25(b) duty to advise is in fact discharged by West Virginia courts at the point of acquittal or dismissal, and therefore whether the packet should tell participants they were entitled to be told about this remedy at the time. The statute was read at source and the duty is unambiguous; the practice is not established and does not change what is generated.

openLegalQuestions.question: Section 61-11-26(r) provides that a person who had a sentence reduction under the repealed § 61-11B-1 et seq. 'may petition the court of record to have the criminal offense reduction order converted into an order of expungement', and that on verification the court shall enter an order of expungement. That is a participant-facing petition with mandatory relief on verification, and it is not inventoried as a mechanism in the controlling review, so it has no source slot and no node here. It is surfaced rather than modelled, because creating an eleventh relief track would break the adopted ten-slot structure.

Open question blocks release (venue): Venue on a multi-county conviction petition. The controlling review states that S.B. 562 (2020) allows a person seeking expungement of convictions in more than one county to file in his or her county of residence. Section 61-11-26 was read in full at source on 2026-08-06 and the current text does not contain a residence-county venue option: subsections (a)(1) and (a)(2) both say 'petition the circuit court in which the conviction or convictions occurred', the subsection (d) proviso requires a multiple-misdemeanour petition to 'identify and group such information by circuit court, as applicable', and § 61-11-26a(a) says 'may petition the circuit court or circuit courts in which the conviction or convictions occurred'. Read together the current text supports one petition covering several counties, grouped by circuit court and served on the prosecuting attorney of each county of conviction, but it does not name a residence-county forum. Venue for the single-county case is unaffected and unambiguous. Until counsel resolves this, the packet directs a multi-county participant to the circuit court of conviction and adds a local-check instruction rather than promising a residence-county filing.

Open question blocks release (eligibility_branch): Whether relief under § 60A-4-407 or § 17C-5-2b counts against the once-per-lifetime limit in § 61-11-26. Section 61-11-26(o) by its terms reaches only §§ 61-11-26 and 61-11-26a, and neither § 60A-4-407 nor § 17C-5-2b cross-references it; both were read in full at source on 2026-08-06 and neither contains a limit referring to § 61-11-26. The textual reading is therefore that they are separate limits in separate statutes, but a participant deciding whether to spend their one lifetime petition needs a settled answer rather than a textual inference.

Open question blocks release (filing_process): Whether the $200 circuit clerk civil filing fee under § 59-1-11(a)(1) is in practice charged in full on an expungement petition in every circuit, and whether any circuit applies an indigency waiver. The statutory amount and its statutory basis are now settled at source; the practice, and whether the ordinary civil indigency affidavit is accepted, is not.

Open question blocks release (eligibility_branch): Whether a conviction arising from the same criminal episode as the offence being set aside counts as a disqualifying other conviction. The controlling review states that it does not, calls the same-episode rule the clearest treatment of any single doctrine in the series and directs that it be preserved in the engine. The enacted text of Oregon Laws 2025 chapter 349, read at the Oregon Legislature's own channel on 2026-08-06, reads the other way on its face: ORS 137.225(7)(a)(B) disqualifies a person convicted of any other offence within the applicable period "whether or not the other conviction is for conduct associated with the same criminal episode". The enacted text does carve out motor vehicle violations, unlawful possession of a controlled substance constituting a drug enforcement misdemeanour, and under ORS 137.225(7)(b) a single non-motor-vehicle violation; the Oregon Judicial Department's own packet describes the carve-out the same way, as "except traffic violations or a single violation offense", and does not mention same-episode convictions. Neither reading is adopted here and no eligibility statement is made where a second conviction from the same episode is in play.

Open question blocks release (participant_instructions): The current Oregon State Police record-check fee. ORS 137.225(2)(d) as enacted leaves the figure to the department, capped at actual cost, so the review's reported figure of about $33 per conviction cannot be confirmed from the statute and the department's current schedule was not obtained. The statute does settle one thing the review did not have: where the department performs only one record check it may charge only one fee regardless of how many counties the person files in.

The controlling review describes Oregon Laws 2025 chapter 395 section 1 as a general rule that expired judgment remedies for monetary obligations in any judgment of conviction count as sentence completion. scopeRestrictions: Expungement in South Dakota is sealing, not destruction, and the statute expressly says it does not imply physical destruction of records.

A nonpublic disposition record survives with the Division of Criminal Investigation for use by law enforcement, prosecutors and courts, including for sentencing on later offences, future SIS eligibility and habitual-offender determinations. This is the single most important disclosure in South Dakota.
South Dakota is not a broad adult conviction-expungement state and must never be described as one.

Pricing honesty. The UJS publishes the full packet, detailed instructions, a Guide and File document generator and a Self-Help Center with staff contact options, all free. LegalEase adds value through eligibility screening, the entire-dismissal analysis, arrest-record counting and expectation-setting, and should not charge as though it were producing documents the state already produces for nothing.

Open question blocks release (eligibility_branch): What the December 1, 2026 version of § 19.2-392.2 does to this track. Read at source on 2026-08-06, the later version replaces the subsection A gateway with any person 'arrested, charged, summonsed, or indicted' for an infraction, crime or civil offence who 'is not ultimately convicted, provided that no stipulation of facts sufficient to find guilt was entered or the court did not determine the facts sufficient to find guilt but deferred adjudication or disposition to a later date'. That codifies the Dotson limit in the statute, extends the route to infractions, and adds a sentence to subsection C permitting a single petition to cover multiple charges arising out of separate transactions or occurrences, which the current version does not allow. It also provides that unavailability of the arrest information alone is not a basis for refusing expungement, and requires an objecting Commonwealth's Attorney to state the basis. The packet must be rebuilt for that version before it takes effect.
